metadata.title: Measurement Properties of Non-cognitive scales in the Polish Follow-up Study on PIAAC (POSTPIAAC) (EN)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses the Polish Follow-up Study on PIAAC (postPIAAC) and combines postPIAAC background/personality data with PIAAC proficiency estimates. Weighting follows PIAAC guidelines: the final postPIAAC weight is based on the person base weight from PIAAC, then adjusted for non-response using classification-tree adjustment cells that are homogeneous in response rates. Calibration targets replicate PIAAC population estimates with respect to age, gender and proficiency score, and the study also computes paired jackknife replicate weights to support variance estimation. The manuscript does not report a single explicit weight variable name (e.g., W_FSTUWT), but it clearly states that complex survey design and sampling weights were accounted for in the estimations.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper reports that correlations are averaged across ten plausible values and that regressions use the first plausible value for numeracy, but it does not describe a full missing-data strategy (e.g., whether missing covariates/outcomes were handled via listwise deletion, imputation, or other methods). Because the analysis relies on plausible values and complex survey estimation, missing-data handling is a methodological detail that is not fully documented in the provided text, representing a reporting gap rather than a design feature.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Analyses are based on postPIAAC respondents who were PIAAC participants living in Poland during the postPIAAC fieldwork (Oct 2014–Feb 2015). From 9,366 initial PIAAC respondents, 5,224 completed postPIAAC interviews; of these, 4,551 completed the Big Five and 5,121 completed the Grit tests, with age/gender/education information. The study then further selects individuals with valid answers to relevant outcome questions, yielding a working sample of 4,454 for life outcomes; job-quality outcomes are restricted further to employed persons with appropriate data (job satisfaction n=3,026; wages n=2,059). For economic outcomes, top and bottom 1% of the wage distribution are excluded and categories with frequency below 5% are merged with neighboring categories for ordinal outcomes.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD report evaluates the psychometric measurement properties of two non-cognitive scales—BFI-S (Big Five Inventory-Short) and Grit-S—in the Polish Follow-up Study on PIAAC (postPIAAC). The study uses a representative adult sample in Poland and applies IRT-based item diagnostics (graded response model), reliability analyses (e.g., omega coefficients), confirmatory factor analysis for structural validity, and multigroup measurement invariance testing (configural/metric/scalar/latent means using delta CFI). For discriminant validity, it compares personality factor scores against PIAAC literacy and numeracy proficiency, finding very weak associations, suggesting the constructs are distinct. For criterion validity, it estimates associations between personality traits and multiple life outcomes (education, labour market participation/employment, job satisfaction, wages, health, trust, life satisfaction) using multivariate regression models (linear, logit, ordered logit) with complex survey weights and plausible values for numeracy. The report concludes that measurement quality is only partially satisfactory (especially for reverse-worded items and full scalar invariance), but personality measures still add predictive power for several policy-relevant outcomes, with limited incremental gains beyond the Big Five for Grit.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is a measurement/criterion-validity assessment using psychometric modeling (IRT, CFA/MCFA, reliability, invariance) and multivariate regression for associations with outcomes; it does not train or evaluate machine-learning predictive models. Consequently, the schema’s ML-specific fields (ml_techniques and main_findings as ML target rows) are intentionally left empty, while the outcome_summary captures the substantive results. The report is also single-country (Poland) and focuses on scale properties and measurement equivalence rather than algorithmic prediction.
